description.narrative: The Australia-Indonesia Partnership for Infrastructure, also known as Kemitraan Indonesia Australia untuk Infrastruktur (KIAT), supports sustainable and inclusive economic growth in Indonesia through improved access to infrastructure for all people. KIAT provides technical assistance and advisory services to the Government of Indonesia to improve infrastructure policy, planning and delivery. KIAT also supports high quality infrastructure project preparation for financing by the private sector, Multilateral Development Banks (MDBs) and/or the Government of Indonesia.

title.narrative: Mid-term Review of the Indonesia-Australia Partnership for Infrastructure

description.narrative: Australia through Gender Equality and Social Inclusion in Infrastructure (GESIT) grants program provided funding and technical assistance to 18 civil society organisations (8 women’s rights organisations, and 10 organisations for persons with disability) across 10 districts to strengthen their capacity to promote inclusive infrastructure. Through this program CSOs and Local Governments worked together to undertake accessibility assessments and identify opportunities to promote gender equality in infrastructure works and services. During the reporting period 5 infrastructure accessibility assessments were conducted in 5 locations: Belitung, Probolinggo, West Lombok, Wonosobo, and Pesisir Selatan. The assessments support future inclusive infrastructure capital works investments. In addition, during the reporting period, 8 CSOs managed to collaborate with the 5 Local Governments in drafting and enacting 14 new inclusive regulations to support inclusive infrastructure policy reform

Australia, through Gender Equality and Social Inclusion in Infrastructure (GESIT), supported grants program with CSOs and organisations for people with disabilities (OPDs). 10 organisations of persons with disabilities have received funds and technical assistance to improve their management skills, networking, and ability to advocate for more inclusive infrastructure policies. A learning event was held in October 2023, and grantees developed improved planning, budgeting, and advocacy processes. Participants were also introduced to safeguard concepts and media engagement strategies. The event enabled grantees to share experience in advocating for improved local regulations and policies relating to inclusive infrastructure. By June 2024, 4 organisations of persons with disabilities in 4 cities (West Lombok, Wonosobo, Probolinggo, and Belitung) has supported the enactment of 12 new disability inclusive infrastructure policies at district and village levels

title.narrative: Climate adaptation, mitigation, environment and biodiversity

description.narrative: Australia, through the Performance-Based Grant (PBG) program, supported the development of Climate Change Adaptation Action Plans (CAAPs) in 5 water utilities across Java and Sumatra, with combined utility service areas of 1.652 million people. ‍ The CAAPs were based on a risk assessment of the impact of existing and potential future hazards across utility networks. The assessments found that climate-related hazards such as floods, landslides and drought have already impacted both the quality and quantity of water supply and the integrity of treatment, transmission, and distribution systems. ‍ The CAAPs allow the utilities to prioritise and estimate the cost of actions for future infrastructure investment required to enhance the climate resilience of their facilities.

Gender Equality and Social Inclusion in Infrastructure (GESIT): The GESIT program has provided grants and intensive capacity-building support to 10 local Organisations of Persons with Disabilities (OPDs) across 10 regions in Indonesia. This support has equipped OPDs to conduct policy research, formulate recommendations, and engage effectively in public consultations. Within the reporting period, grantees participated in 279 formal policy discussions, including musrenbang (participatory development planning meeting).. This engagement contributed to the enactment of 39 inclusive regulations, including 18 on inclusive development, 18 on water supply management, and 3 on inclusive infrastructure. Regulations are being implemented through, for example, accessibility upgrades at a health centre in Alassapi village, East Java, and inclusive employment measures in Wonosobo. Through small grants and capacity-building, the influence of Civil Society Organization (CSOs) and OPDs is being strengthened in local policy processes. These results demonstrate how targeted capacity building to OPDs can strengthen their ability to participate effectively in infrastructure decision-making and promote equitable access through policy and service delivery reforms at the local level.

KIAT provided advice to improve the engagement of women and people with disabilities in public decision-making process across 11 activities during the reporting period. One relevant example was KIAT’s Gender Equality and Social Inclusion in Infrastructure (GESIT) activity, which engaged women and people with disabilities in local infrastructure planning, implementation, and governance through grants to 8 women’s Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) and 10 Organisations of People with Disabilities (OPDs). Support resulted in CSOs and OPDs successfully advocating for issuance of 39 separate local regulations on inclusive infrastructure across 10 districts. CSOs and OPDs have been empowered to engage with existing local multi-stakeholder forums, such as Road Traffic and Transport Forums and Water Customer Forums, to collaborate with decision-makers in making local infrastructure more inclusive. In 2 instances this has resulted in local water utilities providing discounted tariffs for persons with disability. Additionally, one women’s CSO has helped establish a village-owned enterprise to refill drinking water for customers. These examples serve as demonstrations to other CSOs and OPDs of the impact they can have by engaging with technical agencies and village heads, and the opportunities to employ women and people with disabilities in local infrastructure development.

On 25 October 2023, National Development Planning Agency (Bappenas) issued the Ministerial Regulation No.7/2023 introducing important regulatory reforms to simplify the Public-Private Partnership (PPP) process in the infrastructure sector. The new regulation replaces Ministerial Regulation 4/2015 and focusses on red-tape reduction measures for streamlining PPP project identification, planning, preparation, procurement, and management. Developed with Australian technical assistance these measures will support increased private sector investment in infrastructure in Indonesia. Other ministries are harmonising their PPP regulations with the Bappenas Ministerial Regulation No.7/2023, with Australia support.

The Gender Equality and Social Inclusion in Infrastructure (GESIT) program delivered through KIAT provides targeted funding to local women’s organisations to strengthen their role in infrastructure-related policymaking. These organisations, with a primary focus on gender equality and women’s empowerment, are supported to conduct advocacy, engage with local governments, and promote inclusive infrastructure practices. Between July 2024 and June 2025, GESIT disbursed approximately AUD 365,000 across 8 local women’s organisations in 8 regions. The funding supported efforts such as inclusive planning for sanitation, road and transport service accessibility improvements, and gender-responsive budgeting. Recipient organisations included Aisyiyah, IWAPI, Muslimat NU, and KOPPATARA, each of which are recognised for playing a role in advancing women’s rights at the local level. Through GESIT grants, women-led organisations are actively shaping infrastructure dialogue and contributing to more equitable public investment decisions. GESIT demonstrates how targeted funding for gender-focused institutions can strengthen inclusive governance and service delivery in Indonesia’s infrastructure sector.

description.narrative: The Palembang City Sanitation Project (PCSP) supported Government of Indonesia to strengthen sanitation services through infrastructure investment and technical assistance. The project built a Wastewater Treatment Plant (WWTP), technical support for project management, procurement, financial management, engineering design, safeguards, and climate resilience. Completed in October 2023 and inaugurated by President Widodo, the WWTP is fully operational as of April 2025, treating 657 m³ of wastewater per day from 697 property connections and benefiting approx. 4,380 people. Network expansion and household connections are ongoing. ‍ National Sanitation Hibah Program (NSHP), implemented from June 2023 to April 2025, aimed to improve urban sanitation infrastructure across 10 Local Governments (LGs) in Indonesia. Supported by the Ministry of Public Works, NSHP constructed 3,683 household connections (106.3% of target). GOI disbursed IDR21 billion in grants, laying strong foundations for sustainability, inclusion, and future scale-up. ‍ The Revitalising Informal Settlements and their Environments (RISE) activity provided inclusive, climate-resilient water and sanitation infrastructure in 5 informal settlements in Makassar city. It improved services for over 1,400 residents (710 women, 756 men, and 18 people with disabilities), across 349 households, enhancing public health, reducing environmental hazards, and promoting inclusive urban development.

title.narrative: Climate adaptation, mitigation, environment and biodiversity

description.narrative: The Performance-Based Grant (PBG) activity improved the performance of water utilities (PDAMs) in Indonesia through grants and technical assistance. Nine PDAMs implemented energy efficiency measures, including the installation of Variable Speed Drives, optimisation of pump operations, and replacement of inefficient motors. These efforts led to 901,203 kWh in energy savings, equivalent to 720,962 tCO2e reductions in greenhouse gas emissions. At the same time, non-revenue water was reduced by over 10.7 million cubic metres, significantly reducing energy consumption across utilities. Five PDAMs developed Climate Change Adaptation Action Plans (CCAAPs) to guide climate-resilient infrastructure planning. The PBG experience demonstrates how practical infrastructure investments can deliver measurable climate mitigation and adaptation benefits while strengthening service delivery and utility efficiency.

The Provincial Government of Bali has commenced the development of feasibility studies for 2 electric bus rapid transit (eBRT) corridors, based on an earlier Australia-supported Sustainable Urban Mobility Plan (SUMP) for the broader Sarbagita metropolitan area. The feasibility studies are expected to lead to investments by the Government of Indonesia and multilateral donors. The anticipated development of the eBRT corridors (and implementation of the broader SUMP) will improve the availability of electrified public transportation services in the selected corridors, helping to reduce traffic congestion and associated air pollution, and support economic development in the Sarbagita metropolitan area which is home to 2.9 million people and visited by around 4 million tourists annually

The Sarbagita electric Bus Rapid Transit (eBRT) corridor planning and project preparation activity is intended to improve accessibility and liveability in Bali’s metropolitan area across 2 priority transport corridors. The project, first identified through KIAT support for a Sustainable Urban Mobility Plan (SUMP) for Bali in 2022, involves design support and a feasibility study for a 53 km electric bus rapid transit system integrated with other modes (G20 Principles 1 and 6). The design includes universal access features, improved safety, and accommodates women, people with disabilities, and the elderly (G20 Principle 5). Climate change mitigation is central, with the project contributing to Bali’s 2045 net zero target through electrification (G20 Principle 4). KIAT conducted a climate and disaster risk assessment, IFC-compliant ESIA, and a GEDSI assessment to inform the final design (G20 Principles 3, 4, and 5). Capacity building supported the Bali Government on technical, financial, and governance aspects. A soft market sounding was conducted to engage private investors, and discussions are ongoing around the potential for investment from Export Finance Australia (EFA). The final preliminary design was completed and accepted by the Bali Government in December 2024.

The objective of Australia’s Gender Equality and Social Inclusion in Infrastructure (GESIT) grants program in Indonesia is to increase the participation of women and people with disability in inclusive infrastructure planning, design and delivery. The grants program supports 10 women’s organisations in 10 districts across Indonesia to strengthen civil society collaboration with local governments and advocate for more inclusive district-level regulations. In West Lombok, advocacy by the Indonesian Businesswomen’s Association led to a new regulation being approved in December 2023, which mandated women’s representation in local infrastructure development planning and implementation. GESIT partners are also engaging with the private sector to increase opportunities for women to gain safe and suitable work on local infrastructure projects. The program is delivered through the Indonesia–Australia Infrastructure Partnership.

To address persistent gaps in private sector investment, the Government of Indonesia has recently adopted 2 new infrastructure financing mechanisms - Limited Concession Schemes (LCS) and Land Value Capture (LVC) - through Presidential regulations issued in August 2024. These reforms were supported by KIAT through technical studies and advisory inputs on international best practices. LCS enables the recycling of public assets by allowing private operation of existing infrastructure, while LVC captures a portion of increased land and property value resulting from public infrastructure investment. Together, these models improve project bankability, attract institutional investors, and reduce exposure to construction risk. New regulations have been adopted to formalise LCS and LVC as part of Indonesia’s infrastructure finance framework, offering alternative pathways to mobilise sustainable private investment. This reflects a significant improvement in national infrastructure financing regulation and policy, and was directly informed by Australian technical assistance to enhance Indonesia’s infrastructure delivery and investment climate.
